questions.q: What is an LLM's knowledge cutoff?
options: A setting users can toggle to extend the model's knowledge
A rate limit on how many questions can be asked per day
The date after which the model has no training data, and therefore no knowledge of anything that happened or was published afterward
The maximum length of text the model can process in one request
questions.explain: A model's knowledge comes entirely from its training data, which has a fixed end date. It cannot know about events, documents, or facts that appeared after that date.

questions.q: Why can't an LLM simply be retrained constantly to stay current?
options: It would violate the model's license agreement
Training a frontier model takes significant time and compute, so it can't realistically happen continuously
Retraining is instant and cheap, so this isn't actually a limitation
Models are not capable of being retrained more than once
questions.explain: Full retraining is a months-long, resource-intensive process, which is exactly why every deployed model is already somewhat out of date by the time it ships.

questions.q: What is a hallucination, mechanically speaking?
options: A fluent, confident, factually incorrect output — a predictable consequence of next-token prediction when the model doesn't actually know the answer
A memory leak in the model's software
A random, rare bug that is unrelated to how the model generates text
A warning message the model displays when it is uncertain
questions.explain: The model keeps predicting the most statistically plausible next tokens even when it lacks real knowledge, producing text that reads exactly as confidently as a correct answer.

questions.q: In the vendor-contract example in this lesson, why did the model's answer come out wrong?
options: It deliberately lied to the user
It had retrieved the wrong contract from a database
The question was phrased ambiguously
It had never been trained on that specific contract, so it pattern-matched to what vendor contracts typically say instead of the actual document
questions.explain: With no retrieval step, the model has no access to the real contract text, so it falls back on generic patterns from its training data and presents a guess as fact.

questions.q: What is the core gap that retrieval-augmented generation is designed to close?
options: The fact that LLMs cannot generate text in multiple languages
The lack of a live connection between the model and real source documents at the moment it answers
The inability of a model to format its output as JSON
The high cost of running any language model at all
questions.explain: Both the knowledge-cutoff and hallucination problems trace back to the model only having its frozen weights with no real-time access to actual source text — which is exactly what RAG supplies.
